notes.meaning: Jesus gathered His twelve chosen followers and gave them both the right and the power to act in His name. He sent them out equipped to drive out all evil spirits and to heal sicknesses. Luke separates demons from ordinary diseases, showing that evil spirits and bodily illnesses are not the same thing.

Jesus sent the Twelve to tell people that God's royal rule had arrived and to heal those who were sick. The preaching brought the message of God's grace, and the healing showed His love and proved their words were true. Word and deed went together in their work.

Jesus told them not to pack extra supplies or carry money for the trip. They were not to look like beggars collecting coins or worry about their physical needs. Travelling light taught them to trust God to care for them through the people they served.

When they arrived in a town, they were to stay in the first home that welcomed them until they finished their work there. Moving from house to house looking for better food or softer beds would look greedy and hurt their hosts. Staying in one place showed contentment and respect.

If a town refused to welcome the apostles, they were to shake the town's dust off their sandals as they walked away. Jewish people did this when leaving pagan lands to show they wanted no part in their sins. Doing this warned the town that they were leaving them to God's judgment for rejecting His good news.

The apostles obeyed Jesus and traveled through the surrounding villages. They shared the good news of the gospel and healed sick people everywhere they went. They carried out the very same work their Master had been doing.

King Herod Antipas heard about everything taking place and felt troubled and confused. People were trying to explain who Jesus was, guessing He might be John the Baptist raised from the dead, Elijah returned from heaven, or an ancient prophet who had come back. Herod had an uneasy conscience because he had murdered John.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church writers noted that Luke presents Herod as doubtful and confused by the rumors, while the public were the ones claiming John had risen.

notes.meaning: Herod reminded himself that he had already cut off John's head, so he wondered who this new miracle worker could be. He kept trying to catch sight of Jesus. Yet he wanted to see Him out of curiosity and fear rather than a genuine desire to repent.

When the apostles finished their journey, they came back and reported all their deeds to Jesus. He then led them away privately to the countryside near Bethsaida so they could rest. Good workers need quiet times to refresh their bodies and pray.

The crowds learned where Jesus had gone and hurried after Him. Even though they interrupted His quiet rest, Jesus welcomed them warmly. He taught them about God's kingdom and cured every person who needed healing.

As the sun began to set, the Twelve urged Jesus to send the people away to find food and places to sleep in nearby farms and villages. They knew they were in an empty, lonely area with no market. Their advice seemed practical, since they could not imagine how so many could be fed.

Jesus challenged the disciples by telling them to feed the crowd themselves. They answered that they had only five small loaves of bread and two fish, which was nowhere near enough unless they went to buy food. Jesus used their small supply to test their faith and show human helplessness.

About five thousand men were present, not counting women and children. Jesus instructed His disciples to have the people sit down in orderly rows of about fifty each. The disciples obeyed, arranging the large crowd into groups like guests at a banquet.

Jesus took the five loaves and two fish, looked up toward heaven, and gave thanks to God. He broke the bread into pieces and handed them to the disciples to distribute to the crowd. This showed that God is the provider of daily bread, and the food multiplied through Jesus' power.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The actions of taking, blessing, breaking, and giving the bread point ahead to the Eucharist, the sacred meal where Christ feeds His people with spiritual food through the hands of His ministers.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern readers suggest no physical miracle happened, but that the crowd was inspired by Jesus to share the food they had secretly brought with them.

notes.meaning: Everyone ate until they were completely full. Afterwards, the disciples gathered twelve baskets full of leftover crusts and pieces so nothing was wasted. This proved that Christ provides more than enough to meet every need.

Jesus was praying in a quiet place away from the crowd, with His disciples near Him. When He finished praying, He asked them who the crowds believed He was. He brought up public opinion to prepare His disciples to state their own conviction.

The disciples reported that people thought Jesus was John the Baptist, Elijah, or another ancient prophet back from the dead. The crowds respected Jesus as a great man of God, but they still failed to see that He was far greater than any prophet.

Jesus then asked His disciples directly who they believed He was. Speaking for the group, Peter declared that Jesus is the Christ of God, the long-promised King chosen and anointed by God. This confession showed their firm trust in Him even when the rest of the country remained confused.

differ.view: Luke omits any special blessing given to Peter here, which shows that Peter was not given supreme rank or governing authority over the other apostles.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars argue that the phrase 'the Christ of God' reflects the developed language of the early church rather than the exact words originally spoken.

notes.meaning: Jesus firmly ordered His disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Messiah. The Jewish people expected a military king to overthrow the Roman government, and announcing His title too soon would cause political rebellion. His true mission as the Messiah had to be fulfilled through suffering and rising again before it was widely proclaimed.
